passage: In the computer lab, Sharmila taped a sheet to the wall: "Week 3: something that works." Her teammate Jaya frowned at it. "But we planned face recognition." "That comes later," said Sharmila. "First, a rough but running attendance system. A student's name goes in, a tick goes into a table, a teacher can see it. Nothing fancy." For three weeks they built only that, taking turns at the keyboard. On day 21 they clicked through it for their guide, and it worked, though the screen looked plain. "Now the face part," said Jaya, and this time she sounded sure. Even if the semester ran short, there was already a demo to show. Sharmila took the sheet down and wrote "Week 4: faces" beneath.

qa.q: What did Sharmila tape to the wall?
qa.a: She taped a sheet reading 'Week 3: something that works.'

qa.q: What is Jaya feeling when she first sees the sheet?
qa.a: Jaya feels doubtful and a bit disappointed, frowning because they had planned face recognition.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Sharmila and Jaya use if they still feel unsure about starting simple, and why?
qa.a: They could sketch the full design on paper first and mark the smallest working slice, because that keeps the big plan visible while still delivering a demo early.

qa.q: How might their guide see the plain first version?
qa.a: Their guide sees something that works and can be clicked through, which is more reassuring than a large plan with nothing to demonstrate.

grounding: Shows building a simple working version first, adding later features afterwards, so a demo exists even if time runs short.

passage:
Dear Ganga Chechi,
Last year you told me, "Get something working first, then make it clever." I thought you were being boring. You were right.
Our final-year project is an attendance system for the college. The plan had face recognition, automatic reports, a parent app, everything. But after your advice, we built the plainest possible version first: teachers tap names on a tablet, it saves them, and it shows who is absent. It took us three weeks.
Then we added face recognition, which took two months and broke three times. Then reports.
Last week our guide moved our demo two weeks earlier. Other teams panicked. We didn't, because the basic version had worked since August. We showed that, plus face recognition in one classroom.
Thank you, Chechi. Next time I'll call it wise, not boring.
Love,
Elizabeth

qa.q: How long did the plain version take?
How did Elizabeth feel when the demo was moved earlier?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt calm and a little proud while other teams panicked, since the basic version had worked since August.

qa.q: What else could the team do before the final demo?
qa.a: They could test face recognition in more classrooms and keep the basic tap-names version ready as a backup.

qa.q: How might Ganga Chechi feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Ganga Chechi would likely feel pleased and amused that the boring advice turned out to be wise.

grounding: Shows a team building a bare working attendance system in three weeks before adding face recognition and reports, so a demo exists when time runs short.

passage: Our final-year project? Okay. I'm Kalyani, and I'll tell you the part nobody puts in the report. Asif, my teammate, wanted to start with face recognition, because that's the exciting bit. I said, first let's build something ugly that works. So in three weeks we made a web page where the teacher types the roll numbers of students present, it saves them, and it shows who's absent. No faces. Asif called it "a glorified register." Then we started the face part. It was brilliant in the lab and terrible under classroom tube lights. Two weeks before the external demo, the camera module stopped working completely. Asif looked sick. I said, "We still have the glorified register." We demoed that, showed face recognition as a recorded video, and passed comfortably. Asif bought me cutting chai for a week.

qa.q: What did Asif call the plain version?
How did Asif feel when the camera module failed?
qa.a: Asif was dismayed and anxious, looking sick two weeks before the demo.

qa.q: What else could the team have done with the face part?
qa.a: They could have tested it under classroom lighting early, so the problem showed up while there was still time to fix it.

qa.q: How might the external examiner see the demo?
qa.a: The examiner sees a working system plus a video of the face feature, which is enough to pass comfortably even though the camera failed.

grounding: Illustrates a team building a plain working attendance version first and adding face recognition later, so a demo still exists when the camera fails.
